claim: Lamellipodin (Lpd) binds directly to actin filaments in vitro.
source: Lpd takes its name from the dynamic lamellipodial actin networks to which it localizes in vivo, even in the absence of Ena/VASP proteins or free actin filament barbed ends (Krause et al., 2004). This tenacious localization to leading edge actin networks suggested that Lpd might interact directly with actin filaments, so we tested this idea by simultaneously visualizing monomeric GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and individual actin filaments in vitro by Total Internal Reflection Fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by TIRF microscopy experiments showing GFP-Lpd850−1250aa decorating actin filaments (Figure 1A,B), and by co-sedimentation assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).

claim: The dissociation equilibrium constant (Kd) for GFP-Lpd850−1250aa binding to actin filaments in 50 mM KCl buffer is 255 ± 2 nM.
source: In buffer containing 50 mM KCl, the GFP-labeled, monomeric Lpd construct uniformly decorated actin filaments, with a measured dissociation equilibrium constant (Kd) of 255 ± 2 nM (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: Measured directly from TIRF microscopy experiments quantifying GFP-Lpd850−1250aa binding to actin filaments at various concentrations (Figure 1C).

claim: Lpd binding to filamentous actin is weakened by higher concentrations of KCl.
source: Consistent with a weak electrostatic interaction, Lpd binding to filamentous actin grew progressively weaker in buffers containing higher concentrations of KCl. In the presence of 100 mM KCl, interaction between monomeric Lpd and single actin filaments were undetectable by TIRF-M (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing loss of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa binding to actin filaments at 100 mM KCl (Figure 1B).

claim: The interaction between Lpd and actin filaments is electrostatic in nature.
source: Consistent with a weak electrostatic interaction, Lpd binding to filamentous actin grew progressively weaker in buffers containing higher concentrations of KCl.
evidence: Inferred from the salt-dependent binding behavior where higher ionic strength reduces binding.

claim: The C-terminal region of human Lpd (residues 850–1250) is highly basic with an isoelectric point (pI) of 9.97.
source: The carboxy-terminal region of human Lpd (residues 850–1250) is highly basic, with an isoelectric point (pI) of 9.97 (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Calculated using EXPASY ProtParam tool as stated in Materials and methods.

claim: Mutating all 44 basic amino acid residues in the C-terminal actin-binding region of Lpd to alanines abolishes filament binding.
source: Mutating all 44 basic amino acid residues in the C-terminal ABR of Lpd to alanines (to create Lpd(44A)850−1250aa) abolished filament binding (Figure 1D), but had no effect on the ability of this construct to bind to Ena/VASP proteins (unpublished results).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing GFP-Lpd(44A)850−1250aa does not bind actin filaments (Figure 1D).

claim: The distribution of basic residues in the C-terminal region of Lpd is evolutionarily conserved among Lpd homologs.
source: The distribution of basic residues in this region is evolutionarily conserved among Lpd homologs, but is not conserved in other Ena/VASP-binding proteins, such as Rap1-GTP-interacting adaptor molecule (RIAM), zyxin, or ActA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown by protein sequence alignment and pI comparison across species (Figure 2A,B).

claim: Full-length Lpd forms homo-dimers in solution via a coiled-coil motif and interactions in the tandem RA-PH domains.
source: Structural studies indicate that full-length (FL) Lpd forms homo-dimers in solution, via both a coiled-coil motif and interactions in the tandem RA-PH domains (Depetris et al., 2009; Chang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Dimeric GFP-LZ-Lpd binds more strongly to filamentous actin than monomeric GFP-Lpd.
source: Unlike the monomeric Lpd constructs, GFP-LZ-Lpd dimers bound to single actin filaments in both low- and high-salt buffers (100 mM KCl; Figure 1G). Similarly, dimeric Lpd bound more strongly to filamentous actin, both 'native' and phalloidin stabilized, as compared to monomeric Lpd in a co-sedimentation assay (Figure 1H,I and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy (Figure 1G) and co-sedimentation assays (Figure 1H,I).

claim: The stoichiometry of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa binding to actin is approximately one Lpd molecule to at least two actin protomers.
source: Based on the ratio of Lpd:Actin sedimented under saturating conditions, we estimate a stoichiometry of one GFP-Lpd850−1250aa to at least two actin protomers.
evidence: Calculated from co-sedimentation assay data (Figure 1H,I).

claim: Oligomeric his10GFP-Lpd850−1250aa particles bind and diffuse linearly along the sides of actin filaments.
source: In our TIRF assay we observed oligomeric his10GFP-Lpd850−1250aa particles bind and diffuse linearly along the sides of actin filaments (Figure 1J), an activity we previously observed for tetrameric Cy3-VASP constructs (Hansen and Mullins, 2010).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing diffusion along filaments (Figure 1J).

claim: Lpd-coated small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) bind tightly to individual actin filaments in vitro.
source: Finally, we observed enhanced filament binding when we coupled freshly gel-filtered, monomeric his10GFP-Lpd850−1250aa to small unilamellar vesicles (SUVs) containing DOGS-NiNTA lipids (Figure 1K). These Lpd-coated SUVs bound tightly to individual actin filaments in vitro, demonstrating that oligomerization and/or clustering of Lpd850−1250aa promotes stable actin filament binding, even in near physiological salt concentrations.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing Lpd-coated SUVs binding to actin filaments (Figure 1K).

claim: Oligomerization and/or clustering of Lpd850−1250aa promotes stable actin filament binding, even in near physiological salt concentrations.
source: These Lpd-coated SUVs bound tightly to individual actin filaments in vitro, demonstrating that oligomerization and/or clustering of Lpd850−1250aa promotes stable actin filament binding, even in near physiological salt concentrations.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing enhanced binding of oligomeric and membrane-clustered Lpd compared to monomeric Lpd.

claim: Membrane-tethered Lpd significantly slows the rate of actin network assembly on lipid-coated beads.
source: By measuring the length and density of actin comet tails at various times (Figure 3B), we found that membrane-tethered Lpd significantly slowed the rate of actin network assembly (1.5 ± 0.25 µm/min) compared to membrane-tethered GFP alone (7.0 ± 0.48 µm/min; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Measured from actin comet tail growth assays on lipid-coated beads (Figure 3B,C).

claim: Membrane-tethered Lpd polarizes in an actin-dependent manner on the surface of lipid-coated beads.
source: In addition to slowing network growth, membrane-tethered Lpd also polarized in an actin-dependent manner on the surface of LCBs. Similar to the polarization of N-WASP on lipid vesicles in Xenopus egg extract (Co et al., 2007), we found that Scar/WAVE and Lpd constructs become enriched in regions of the membrane most closely associated with the growing actin network.
evidence: Observed in lipid-coated bead assays showing Lpd enrichment at the barbed end attachment zone (Figure 3E).

claim: Both his10Cherry-SCAR and his10GFP-Lpd850−1250aa become concentrated in the barbed end attachment zone within 10 minutes of initiating actin network assembly.
source: Within 10 min of initiating actin network assembly on LCBs, however, both membrane-tethered Scar/WAVE and Lpd constructs (his10GFP-Lpd850−1250aa) became concentrated in the region adjacent to the actin network, a region we refer to as the 'barbed end attachment zone' (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy of lipid-coated beads during actin network assembly (Figure 3E).

claim: Membrane-tethered his10GFP is displaced away from the barbed end attachment zone and becomes concentrated on the opposite side of the microsphere.
source: In contrast, membrane-tethered his10GFP was displaced away from the barbed end attachment zone and became concentrated on the opposite side of the microsphere (Figure 3F).
evidence: Observed by fluorescence microscopy showing GFP exclusion from the actin-rich region (Figure 3F).

claim: Full-length GFP-Lpd1−1250aa localizes predominantly to the leading edge of ruffling membranes in XTC cells.
source: TIRF microscopy imaging of single GFP-Lpd1−1250aa molecules revealed that FL Lpd localizes predominantly to the leading edge of ruffling membranes and cycles on and off the plasma membrane on a subsecond time scale (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in live XTC cells (Figure 4B, Video 1).

claim: GFP-Lpd1−1250aa cycles on and off the plasma membrane on a subsecond time scale.
source: TIRF microscopy imaging of single GFP-Lpd1−1250aa molecules revealed that FL Lpd localizes predominantly to the leading edge of ruffling membranes and cycles on and off the plasma membrane on a subsecond time scale (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Video 1).
evidence: Observed by high temporal resolution TIRF microscopy (Video 1).

claim: Leading edge membrane localization of GFP-Lpd1−1250aa requires dynamic actin assembly and disassembly.
source: Leading edge membrane localization of GFP-Lpd1−1250aa required dynamic actin assembly and disassembly, because acute treatment of cells with a chemical inhibitor cocktail that freezes actin dynamics (JLY drug cocktail: Jasplakinolide, Latrunculin B, and Y27632 Rock kinase inhibitor [Peng et al., 2011]) caused rapid loss of membrane-localized Lpd (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated by drug treatment experiments showing loss of Lpd localization upon freezing actin dynamics (Figure 4C).

claim: GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, which lacks the tandem RA-PH domains, localizes to leading edge membranes in XTC cells.
source: We discovered that not only does GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, which lacks the tandem RA-PH domains, localize to leading edge membranes in XTC cells (Figure 4C), this construct also undergoes retrograde flow with the lamellipodial actin network.
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: GFP-Lpd850−1250aa undergoes retrograde flow with the lamellipodial actin network.
source: We discovered that not only does GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, which lacks the tandem RA-PH domains, localize to leading edge membranes in XTC cells (Figure 4C), this construct also undergoes retrograde flow with the lamellipodial actin network.
evidence: Demonstrated by speckle tracking showing similar velocities for Lpd and actin (Figure 4D-F).

claim: GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and mCherry-Actin move with the same mean velocity: 71.9 ± 17.5 nm/s for Lpd850−1250aa vs 73.5 ± 14 nm/s for actin.
source: Analysis of speckle velocities in XTC cells co-expressing GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and mCherry-Actin revealed that the two proteins move with the same mean velocity: 71.9 ± 17.5 nm/s for Lpd850−1250aa vs 73.5 ± 14 nm/s for actin (Figure 4F, Video 2).
evidence: Measured from speckle tracking analysis in live cells (Figure 4F).

claim: GFP-Lpd850−1250aa simultaneously binds up to four VASP EVH1 domains in solution.
source: By analytical ultracentrifugation, we found that GFP-Lpd850−1250aa simultaneously binds up to four VASP EVH1 domains in solution (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by analytical ultracentrifugation experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: The C-terminal region of Lpd contains six FPPPP peptide sequences, each of which can potentially bind one VASP EVH1 domain.
source: The C-terminal region of Lpd contains six FPPPP peptide sequences, each of which can potentially bind one VASP EVH1 domain.
evidence: Identified from protein sequence analysis (Figure 2A).

claim: The Lpd mutant with all six FPPPP motifs mutated to AAPPP fails to recruit Ena/VASP proteins to lipid-coated beads in vitro.
source: Although the his10-GFP-Lpd(AAPPPx6)850−1250aa mutant failed to recruit Ena/VASP proteins to LCBs in vitro (Figure 5A), the localization of the GFP-Lpd(AAPPPx6)850−1250aa mutant in XTC cells was nearly indistinguishable from GFP-Lpd850−1250aa (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated by lipid-coated bead recruitment assays (Figure 5A).

claim: The localization of GFP-Lpd(AAPPPx6)850−1250aa mutant in XTC cells is nearly indistinguishable from wild-type GFP-Lpd850−1250aa.
source: Although the his10-GFP-Lpd(AAPPPx6)850−1250aa mutant failed to recruit Ena/VASP proteins to LCBs in vitro (Figure 5A), the localization of the GFP-Lpd(AAPPPx6)850−1250aa mutant in XTC cells was nearly indistinguishable from GFP-Lpd850−1250aa (Figure 5B).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5B).

claim: Full-length human Lpd1−1250aa contains 10 potential SH3 domain binding sites, of which four fall within the Lpd850−1250aa construct.
source: FL human Lpd1−1250aa contains 10 potential SH3 domain binding sites (Law et al., 2013), of which four fall within our ABR construct, Lpd850−1250aa (Figure 2A).
evidence: Identified from protein sequence analysis and cited literature (Figure 2A).

claim: The Lpd(SH3*)850−1250aa mutant with mutations in all four SH3 domain binding sites can still localize to the leading edge in XTC cells, but to a lesser extent than wild-type Lpd.
source: This mutant, termed Lpd(SH3*)850−1250aa, could still localize to the leading edge in XTC cells (Figure 5B), but to a lesser extent than wild-type Lpd or the (AAPPP)x6 Lpd mutant which does not bind Ena/VASP EVH1 domains.
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5B).

claim: GFP-Lpd(44A)850−1250aa lacking all lysine and arginine residues fails to concentrate at actin-based membrane protrusions or nascent focal adhesions in XTC cells.
source: Similar to GFP-Lpd(44A)850−1250aa, the GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa construct also failed to concentrate at actin-based membrane protrusion or nascent focal adhesions in XTC cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5B).

claim: GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa, which lacks basic residues between Ena/VASP and Abi1/endophilin binding sites, fails to concentrate at actin-based membrane protrusions or nascent focal adhesions in XTC cells.
source: Similar to GFP-Lpd(44A)850−1250aa, the GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa construct also failed to concentrate at actin-based membrane protrusion or nascent focal adhesions in XTC cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5B).

claim: Lyn-GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, constitutively tethered to the plasma membrane, localizes to the leading edge of actin-based membrane protrusions.
source: Similar to what has previously been observed for membrane tethered ActA-(FPPPP)x4-CAAX (Bear et al., 2002) and soluble GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, described here, Lyn-GFP-Lpd850−1250aa localized to the leading edge of actin-based membrane protrusions (Figure 5D, Video 4).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5D, Video 4).

claim: Lyn-GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa fails to localize to the peripheral regions where Ena/VASP, Abi1, and endophilin are located.
source: Although Lyn-GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa was targeted to the plasma membrane by the palmitoyl lipid anchor, this mutant still failed to localize to the peripheral regions where Ena/VASP, Abi1, and endophilin are located (Figure 5D).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5D).

claim: Lyn-GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa is distributed uniformly across the plasma membrane, similar to membrane-anchored Lyn-GFP lacking Lpd sequences.
source: Localization of Lyn-GFP-Lpd(35A)850−1250aa was identical to that of a membrane-anchored Lyn-GFP construct lacking any Lpd sequences. Both of these constructs were distributed uniformly across the plasma membrane (Figure 5D).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5D).

claim: GFP-PLCδ PH domain distributes uniformly across the plasma membrane of XTC cells.
source: To look for such a polarized lipid distribution we expressed a phosphatidylinositol lipid sensor, based on the pleckstrin-homology domain of phospholipase Cδ (GFP-PLCδ PH). We found that GFP-PLCδ PH distributes uniformly across the plasma membrane of XTC cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy in XTC cells (Figure 5D).

claim: Freezing actin assembly and disassembly with Jasplakinolide and Latrunculin B causes rapid retrograde movement of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa away from the leading edge.
source: First, we simply froze actin assembly and disassembly by adding a mixture of Jasplakinolide and Latrunculin B to cells, without inhibiting myosin activity. Under these conditions we observed rapid retrograde movement of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa away from the leading edge, identical to the movement of mCherry-Actin (Figure 6A, Video 5).
evidence: Observed by time-lapse TIRF microscopy following drug treatment (Figure 6A, Video 5).

claim: Treatment with Cytochalasin D causes a large fraction of leading edge-localized GFP-Lpd850−1250aa to immediately dissociate from the leading edge membrane and flow back with the actin cytoskeleton.
source: When we treated these cells with a 100 nM Cytochalasin D, we observed a large fraction of leading edge-localized GFP-Lpd850−1250aa immediately dissociate from the leading edge membrane and flow back with the actin cytoskeleton (Figure 6B, Video 6).
evidence: Observed by time-lapse TIRF microscopy following Cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 6B, Video 6).

claim: Cytochalasin D treatment causes more dramatic dissociation of GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa from the leading edge membrane compared to monomeric GFP-Lpd850−1250aa.
source: Because GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa binds more strongly to filamentous actin, dissociation from the leading edge membrane was more dramatic following addition of Cytochalasin D (Figure 6C, Video 7).
evidence: Observed by time-lapse TIRF microscopy following Cytochalasin D treatment (Figure 6C, Video 7).

claim: The leading edge localization of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa is regulated, in part, by a direct interaction with free actin filament barbed ends, independent of interactions with Ena/VASP or Abi1/endophilin proteins.
source: Together, these results suggest that the leading edge localization of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa is regulated, in part, by a direct interaction with free actin filament barbed ends, independent of interactions with Ena/VASP or Abi1/endophilin proteins.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing Cytochalasin D-induced dissociation of Lpd mutants that cannot bind Ena/VASP or SH3 domains (Figure 6D,E).

claim: Lpd can bind Ena/VASP proteins and filamentous actin simultaneously.
source: The six VASP-binding 'FPPPP' motifs in the C-terminal region of Lpd do not appear to overlap the cloud of basic residues that mediate actin filament binding (Figure 2A). We, therefore, wondered whether Lpd could bind Ena/VASP proteins and filamentous actin simultaneously.
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing GFP-Lpd850−1250aa causes VASP constructs to associate with actin filaments (Figure 7B).

claim: Several Cy3-labeled VASP constructs (isolated EVH1 domain and two full-length tetrameric actin-binding mutants) fail to bind actin filaments in vitro.
source: To test this idea, we first used TIRF microscopy to demonstrate that several Cy3-labeled VASP constructs—an isolated EVH1 domain and two full length, tetrameric, actin-binding mutants—failed to bind actin filaments (Figure 7A).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing no binding of VASP constructs to actin filaments (Figure 7A).

claim: Addition of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa causes VASP constructs that cannot bind actin to associate with the sides of actin filaments.
source: Addition of GFP-Lpd850−1250aa, however, caused all of these VASP constructs to associate with the sides of actin filaments (Figure 7B).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing colocalization of VASP and Lpd on actin filaments (Figure 7B).

claim: Interaction of tetrameric Cy3-VASP actin-binding mutant with monomeric Lpd produces higher-order VASP clusters visible on the sides of filaments.
source: Interaction of the tetrameric Cy3-VASP actin-binding mutant with the monomeric Lpd construct produced higher-order VASP clusters visible on the sides of the filaments (Figure 7B, arrowheads).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing bright clusters on actin filaments (Figure 7B).

claim: The combined presence of VASP and GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa produces large actin bundles in buffer containing 100 mM KCl.
source: Supporting the notion that Lpd-VASP complexes can synergistically bind actin filaments, we find that the presence of both VASP and GFP-LZ-Lpd results in a large amount of actin filament bundling in the presence of 100 mM KCl (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing actin filament bundling (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Individual actin filaments elongating in the presence of 50 nM tetrameric VASP or 250 nM dimeric GFP-LZ-Lpd alone do not bundle actin filaments in high ionic strength buffer.
source: In contrast, individual actin filaments elongating in the presence of 50 nM tetrameric VASP or 250 nM dimeric GFP-LZ-Lpd alone do not bundle actin filaments in high ionic strength buffer.
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing no bundling with individual proteins (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: The Lpd-VASP interaction can compensate for the weak actin filament binding observed for the individual proteins in buffer containing 100 mM KCl.
source: This means that the Lpd-VASP interaction can compensate for the weak actin filament binding observed for the individual proteins in buffer containing 100 mM KCl.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that VASP and Lpd together cause bundling while individually they do not.

claim: The weak interaction between monomeric GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and filamentous actin is antagonized by the presence of monomeric actin or profilin-actin.
source: The weak interaction between monomeric GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and filamentous actin turns out to be further antagonized by the presence of monomeric actin or profilin-actin (Figure 8A).
evidence: Demonstrated by TIRF microscopy showing reduced Lpd binding to filaments in the presence of monomeric actin (Figure 8A).

claim: Soluble GFP-Lpd850−1250aa and GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa reduce the rate of barbed end actin filament elongation in the presence of 2 µM profilin-actin.
source: Also, we observed a reduction in the rate of barbed end actin filament elongation in the presence 2 µM profilin-actin and soluble GFP-Lpd850−1250aa or GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa (Figure 8B), consistent with Lpd binding to (and partially sequestering) actin monomers.
evidence: Measured from single actin filament elongation assays (Figure 8B).

claim: Dimeric GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa can transiently interact with both the sides and barbed ends of single growing actin filaments.
source: In contrast to monomeric Lpd, dimeric GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa could transiently interact with both the sides and barbed ends of single growing actin filaments (Figure 8D, Video 8).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing Lpd localization on elongating filaments (Figure 8D, Video 8).

claim: Lpd binds well enough to promote filament bundling when present at a near stoichiometric concentration relative to monomeric actin.
source: Although GFP-Lpd and GFP-LZ-Lpd associate more transiently with single actin filaments in the presence of monomeric actin, Lpd binds well enough to promote filament bundling when present at a near stoichiometric concentration relative to monomeric actin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed by TIRF microscopy showing actin filament bundling (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).

claim: GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa decorated actin filaments increase the processivity of barbed end-associated Cy3-VASP tetramers.
source: Fluorescently labeled VASP tetramers accumulate on growing actin filament barbed ends decorated with GFP-LZ-Lpd850−1250aa where they form a stable population (τ1 = 0.58 ± 0.05 s (73%), τ2 = 2.3 ± 0.4 s (27%); Figure 8E–G) that dissociates much more slowly than VASP tetramers observed in the absence of GFP-LZ-Lpd (τ1 = 0.49 ± 0.03 s; Figure 8E–G).
evidence: Measured from single molecule TIRF microscopy experiments analyzing VASP dwell times (Figure 8E-G).

claim: Complexes containing both VASP and Lpd processively track growing actin filament barbed ends at a velocity of 36 ± 9.4 subunits/s.
source: Under these conditions we observed complexes containing both VASP and Lpd processively track growing actin filament barbed ends at a velocity of 36 ± 9.4 subunits/s (Figure 8I, Video 9).
evidence: Measured from single actin filament elongation assays with VASP-Lpd complexes (Figure 8I, Video 9).

claim: The rate at which Lpd-VASP complexes shuttle actin monomers onto free barbed ends is faster than elongation of single actin filaments in the presence of 50 nM tetrameric VASP (25 ± 1.6 subunits/s).
source: The rate at which Lpd-VASP complexes shuttled actin monomers onto free barbed ends was faster than elongation of single actin filaments in the presence of 50 nM tetrameric VASP (25 ± 1.6 subunits/s, Figure 8I).
evidence: Measured from single actin filament elongation assays comparing VASP-Lpd complexes to VASP alone (Figure 8I).

claim: The dwell time for VASP-Lpd tip complexes (τ1 = 33 ± 2 s) is significantly longer compared to single VASP tetramers (τ1 = 0.49 ± 0.03 s).
source: The dwell time for VASP-Lpd tip complexes (τ1 = 33 ± 2 s; Figure 8J) was also significantly longer as compared to single VASP tetramers (τ1 = 0.49 ± 0.03 s; Figure 8F).
evidence: Measured from single molecule TIRF microscopy experiments analyzing complex dwell times (Figure 8J, 8F).

claim: Lpd increases processivity of barbed end-associated VASP tetramers by tethering them to actin filaments.
source: In vitro, Lpd increases processivity of barbed end-associated VASP tetramers by tethering them to actin filaments.
evidence: Demonstrated by experiments showing increased VASP dwell times and processivity in the presence of Lpd (Figure 8E-J).

claim: Ena/VASP proteins are weakly processive actin polymerases that accelerate filament elongation and slow filament capping.
source: One important group of actin regulatory proteins is the Ena/VASP family: weakly processive actin polymerases that accelerate filament elongation and slow filament capping (Barzik et al., 2005; Breitsprecher et al., 2008; Hansen and Mullins, 2010; Breitsprecher et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies characterizing Ena/VASP activity.

claim: Recruitment of Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane often promotes outgrowth of thin, finger-like filopodia and sometimes promotes rapid advance of broad lamellipodial sheets.
source: Recruitment of Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane often promotes outgrowth of thin, finger-like filopodia and sometimes promotes rapid advance of broad lamellipodial sheets (Lanier et al., 1999; Rottner et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Stable localization of Ena/VASP to the plasma membrane requires both the EVH1 and EVH2 domains.
source: Stable localization of Ena/VASP to the plasma membrane requires both the Enabled/VASP homology 1 and 2 domains (EVH1 and EVH2) (Loureiro et al., 2002; Applewhite et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The EVH1 domain is a protein–protein interaction motif that binds proline-rich target sequences (e.g., FPPPP).
source: The EVH1 domain is a protein–protein interaction motif that binds proline-rich target sequences (e.g., FPPPP) (Prehoda et al., 1999), and removal of the EVH1 sequence abolishes localization of Ena/VASP to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane of fibroblasts (Loureiro et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Removal of the EVH1 sequence abolishes localization of Ena/VASP to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane of fibroblasts.
source: The EVH1 domain is a protein–protein interaction motif that binds proline-rich target sequences (e.g., FPPPP) (Prehoda et al., 1999), and removal of the EVH1 sequence abolishes localization of Ena/VASP to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane of fibroblasts (Loureiro et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Interaction with actin filaments is mediated by the EVH2 sequence, which contains an actin binding domain and a tetramerization motif required for polymerase activity.
source: Interaction with actin filaments is mediated by the EVH2 sequence, which contains an actin binding domain (BD) and a tetramerization motif required for polymerase activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Ena/VASP domain structure and function.

claim: When expressed by itself in cells, the EVH2 domain concentrates in lamellipodial actin networks, but fails to achieve the same tight, membrane-proximal localization pattern as the intact protein.
source: When expressed by itself in cells, the EVH2 domain concentrates in lamellipodial actin networks, but fails to achieve the same tight, membrane-proximal localization pattern as the intact protein (Bear et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Cytochalasin D, which caps actin filament barbed ends, rapidly displaces Ena/VASP proteins from the cell periphery.
source: Cytochalasin D, which caps actin filament barbed ends, rapidly displaces Ena/VASP proteins from the cell periphery (Krause et al., 2004; Lacayo et al., 2007; Neel et al., 2009) arguing strongly that free filament ends play a functional role in Ena/VASP localization.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Free filament ends play a functional role in Ena/VASP localization.
source: Cytochalasin D, which caps actin filament barbed ends, rapidly displaces Ena/VASP proteins from the cell periphery (Krause et al., 2004; Lacayo et al., 2007; Neel et al., 2009) arguing strongly that free filament ends play a functional role in Ena/VASP localization.
evidence: Inferred from the effect of Cytochalasin D on Ena/VASP localization.

claim: Ena/VASP binding partners include the bacterial effector ActA, the focal adhesion protein Zyxin, an organizer of dorsal stress fibers palladin, T-cell receptor signaling proteins Fyb/SLAP, axon guidance factors Robo/Sax-3, and the mig-10/RIAM/Lamellipodin (MRL) proteins.
source: Ena/VASP binding partners, which include the bacterial effector ActA (Niebuhr et al., 1997); the focal adhesion protein, Zyxin (Drees et al., 2000); an organizer of dorsal stress fibers, palladin (Boukhelifa et al., 2004; Gateva et al., 2014); T-cell receptor signaling proteins, Fyb/SLAP (Krause et al., 2000); axon guidance factors, Robo/Sax-3 (Bashaw et al., 2000); and the mig-10/RIAM/Lamellipodin (MRL) proteins (Krause et al., 2004; Lafuente et al., 2004), all contain tandem repeats of a high-affinity EVH1 binding sequence: D/E FPPPPXD.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies identifying these binding partners.

claim: All known Ena/VASP binding partners contain tandem repeats of a high-affinity EVH1 binding sequence: D/E FPPPPXD.
source: Ena/VASP binding partners, which include the bacterial effector ActA (Niebuhr et al., 1997); the focal adhesion protein, Zyxin (Drees et al., 2000); an organizer of dorsal stress fibers, palladin (Boukhelifa et al., 2004; Gateva et al., 2014); T-cell receptor signaling proteins, Fyb/SLAP (Krause et al., 2000); axon guidance factors, Robo/Sax-3 (Bashaw et al., 2000); and the mig-10/RIAM/Lamellipodin (MRL) proteins (Krause et al., 2004; Lafuente et al., 2004), all contain tandem repeats of a high-affinity EVH1 binding sequence: D/E FPPPPXD.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A second group of Ena/VASP binding partners, including the formin-family protein Diaphanous and the WAVE regulatory complex, relies on a related, but lower affinity, EVH1-binding motif: LPPPPP.
source: A second group of Ena/VASP binding partners, including the formin-family protein Diaphanous (Grosse et al., 2003; Schirenbeck et al., 2006; Barzik et al., 2014; Bilancia et al., 2014) and the WAVE regulatory complex (Law et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014), relies on a related, but lower affinity, EVH1-binding motif: LPPPPP.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MRL proteins colocalize with Ena/VASP at the plasma membrane of many different cell types in many diverse organisms, both vertebrates and invertebrates.
source: The MRL proteins colocalize with Ena/VASP at the plasma membrane of many different cell types in many diverse organisms, both vertebrates and invertebrates (Krause et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: In the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, the mig-10 protein promotes neurite outgrowth and proper axon guidance.
source: In the nematode, Caenorhabditis elegans, the mig-10 protein promotes neurite outgrowth and proper axon guidance (Manser et al., 1997; Chang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In mammals, Lamellipodin helps determine morphology of neurons and promotes growth of lamellipodial protrusions in a variety of non-neuronal cells.
source: Similarly, in mammals the protein Lamellipodin (Lpd) helps determine morphology of neurons and promotes growth of lamellipodial protrusions in a variety of non-neuronal cells (Michael et al., 2010; Pinheiro et al., 2011; Yoshinaga et al., 2012; Law et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Several MRL proteins, including Lpd, contain a tandem Ras-Association and Pleckstrin Homology (RA-PH) domain which, together with an adjacent coiled-coil region, causes the proteins to form weak homo-dimers in solution.
source: Several MRL proteins, including Lpd, contain a tandem Ras-Association and Pleckstrin Homology (RA-PH) domain which, together with an adjacent coiled-coil region, causes the proteins to form weak homo-dimers in solution (Chang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: The RA-PH domain is structurally homologous to growth factor receptor-binding proteins Grb7, Grb10, and Grb14.
source: The RA-PH domain is structurally homologous to growth factor receptor-binding proteins Grb7, Grb10, and Grb14 (Depetris et al., 2009) but, unlike the Grb proteins, no direct interaction between small GTPases (e.g., Ras or Rho family) and MRL proteins has been reported.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: No direct interaction between small GTPases (e.g., Ras or Rho family) and MRL proteins has been reported.
source: The RA-PH domain is structurally homologous to growth factor receptor-binding proteins Grb7, Grb10, and Grb14 (Depetris et al., 2009) but, unlike the Grb proteins, no direct interaction between small GTPases (e.g., Ras or Rho family) and MRL proteins has been reported.
evidence: Based on absence of reports in the literature.

claim: In vitro, the MRL pleckstrin homology (PH) domain binds phosphatidylinositol lipids: PI(3,4)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P2.
source: In vitro, the MRL pleckstrin homology (PH) domain binds phosphatidylinositol lipids: PI(3,4)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P2 and in vivo the PH domain is thought to target these proteins to the plasma membrane in response to extracellular ligands such as PDGF (Krause et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In vivo, the PH domain is thought to target MRL proteins to the plasma membrane in response to extracellular ligands such as PDGF.
source: In vitro, the MRL pleckstrin homology (PH) domain binds phosphatidylinositol lipids: PI(3,4)P2 and PI(3,4,5)P2 and in vivo the PH domain is thought to target these proteins to the plasma membrane in response to extracellular ligands such as PDGF (Krause et al., 2004; Chang et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MRL proteins have been shown to help recruit Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane.
source: Although the MRL proteins have been shown to help recruit Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane, their effect on Ena/VASP activity has never been characterized.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: The effect of MRL proteins on Ena/VASP activity has never been characterized prior to this study.
source: Although the MRL proteins have been shown to help recruit Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane, their effect on Ena/VASP activity has never been characterized.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the current study's findings.

claim: Results from several studies indicate that the MRL proteins likely have additional, Ena/VASP-independent roles in actin network regulation.
source: In addition, results from several studies indicate that the MRL proteins likely have additional, Ena/VASP-independent roles in actin network regulation (Krause et al., 2004; Lyulcheva et al., 2008; Michael et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lpd can interact directly with artificial lamellipodial actin networks reconstituted in vitro from purified components.
source: We next tested whether Lpd can interact directly with artificial lamellipodial actin networks reconstituted in vitro from purified components (Loisel et al., 1999; Akin and Mullins, 2008).
evidence: Demonstrated by lipid-coated bead actin network assembly assays (Figure 3).

claim: Knockdown of Lpd inhibits lamellipodium formation more potently compared to loss of Ena/VASP proteins.
source: The function of Lpd at the leading edge is not simply to recruit Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane: Knockdown of Lpd inhibits lamellipodium formation more potently compared to loss of Ena/VASP proteins (Bear et al., 2002; Krause et al., 2004) and results in global reduction of lamellipodial actin density (Lyulcheva et al., 2008; Michael et al., 2010; Law et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Knockdown of Lpd results in global reduction of lamellipodial actin density.
source: The function of Lpd at the leading edge is not simply to recruit Ena/VASP proteins to the plasma membrane: Knockdown of Lpd inhibits lamellipodium formation more potently compared to loss of Ena/VASP proteins (Bear et al., 2002; Krause et al., 2004) and results in global reduction of lamellipodial actin density (Lyulcheva et al., 2008; Michael et al., 2010; Law et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both Lpd and Ena/VASP interact with the Scar/WAVE regulatory complex.
source: Recently both Lpd and its binding partners Ena/VASP were found to interact with the Scar/WAVE regulatory complex (Law et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014), an important activator of the Arp2/3 complex at the leading edge.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Scar/WAVE regulatory complex is an important activator of the Arp2/3 complex at the leading edge.
source: Recently both Lpd and its binding partners Ena/VASP were found to interact with the Scar/WAVE regulatory complex (Law et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2014), an important activator of the Arp2/3 complex at the leading edge.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of WAVE complex function.

claim: Interactions between WAVE complex and Lpd/Ena/VASP are mediated by the SH3 domain of Abi1, which binds multiple PxxPxR motifs in the C-terminus of Lpd and the EVH1 domains of Ena/VASP proteins.
source: These interactions are mediated by the SH3 domain of Abi1, a WAVE complex component, which binds multiple PxxPxR motifs in the C-terminus of Lpd and the EVH1 domains of Ena/VASP proteins.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein-protein interactions.

claim: Mutations interfering with WAVE-Lpd binding impaired cell migration in wound closure assays.
source: Mutations interfering with WAVE-Lpd binding impaired cell migration in wound closure assays (Law et al., 2013), demonstrating the functional relevance of this interaction.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study.

claim: Lpd has been implicated in regulating fast endophilin-mediated endocytosis (FEME).
source: Besides its function in regulating lamellipodial actin network assembly, Lpd has also been implicated in regulating FEME (Vehlow et al., 2013; Boucrot et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The C-terminus of Lpd binds to SH3 domains in endophilin using multiple PxxPxR motifs.
source: Similar to the interactions with the WAVE complex, the C-terminus of Lpd binds to SH3 domains in endophilin using multiple PxxPxR motifs.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of protein-protein interactions.

claim: Lpd could function to orchestrate the actin nucleation machinery at the sites of FEME.
source: Because Lpd interacts directly with filamentous actin and multiple actin regulatory proteins, Lpd could function to orchestrate the actin nucleation machinery at the sites of FEME.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the findings of the study.

claim: Local enrichment of Lpd at the plasma membrane can exert a non-linear, cooperative effect on Ena/VASP activity.
source: Because of this effect, local enrichment of Lpd at the plasma membrane can exert a non-linear, cooperative effect on Ena/VASP activity (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that oligomerization enhances Lpd binding to actin and VASP.

claim: Lpd delivers Ena/VASP proteins to growing barbed ends and increases their polymerase activity by tethering them to filaments.
source: We propose that Lpd delivers Ena/VASP proteins to growing barbed ends and increases their polymerase activity by tethering them to filaments.
evidence: Proposed model based on the experimental findings of the study.

claim: This interaction represents one more pathway by which growing actin filaments produce positive feedback to control localization and activity of proteins that regulate their assembly.
source: This interaction represents one more pathway by which growing actin filaments produce positive feedback to control localization and activity of proteins that regulate their assembly.
evidence: Interpretive statement about the broader significance of the findings.

evidence: Stated in Materials and methods section.
